key_concept: Each pituitary hormone (anterior: GH, LH; posterior: vasopressin/ADH, oxytocin) has a specific target action or a disorder linked to its excess.
steps: A. Excess growth hormone: hypersecretion of GH in adults, after the epiphyseal plates have closed, causes acromegaly (severe disfigurement, especially of the face). In children it causes gigantism. So A → III.
B. Luteinizing hormone: the mid-cycle LH surge induces rupture of the Graafian follicle, which is ovulation. LH also helps maintain the corpus luteum. So B → IV.
C. Vasopressin (ADH): this posterior pituitary hormone acts on the distal tubule and collecting duct. It increases reabsorption of water and electrolytes and so reduces diuresis. So C → I.
D. Oxytocin: it stimulates vigorous contraction of the uterine smooth muscle during childbirth and milk ejection from the mammary glands. So D → II.
Combined matching: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II, which is option (2).
why_not_others: Option (1) swaps vasopressin and oxytocin; both are posterior pituitary hormones, so they are easily confused. Options (3) and (4) fail at the first pair, because excess GH gives acromegaly and has nothing to do with uterine contraction or ovulation.
common_trap: Students often swap vasopressin and oxytocin because both are hypothalamic hormones released from the neurohypophysis.
time_saving_tip: Fix A-III (acromegaly), which leaves only options (1) and (2). Then fix D-II (oxytocin causes uterine contraction) to select option (2).
